mainTopic: How many judges sit on the סנהדרי גדולה; the story of אלדד ומידד; how a majority of two can arise; and rules and qualifications for the סנהדרין
overview: The amud finishes the מחלוקת over whether the סנהדרי גדולה has 71 judges (the רבנן, who count משה with the seventy) or 70 (רבי יהודה, who reads each 'with you' differently). A ברייתא then tells the story of אלדד ומידד, who 'remained in the camp'. One view says their names were left in the lottery box. The ברייתא explains משה's lottery and compares it to a similar lottery for the extra בכורות. רבי שמעון says instead that they stayed behind out of humility, and their reward was prophecy that never stopped. The גמרא lists three views on what they prophesied and tests each one against what יהושע and משה said in the פסוקים. It then returns to the משנה's count of 23 judges and asks how a majority of exactly two can ever happen. רבי אבהו answers that it happens once judges are added, or in a court of seventy. The amud ends with rules for the סנהדרין: a unanimous guilty vote frees the defendant, and judges need special qualities and very sharp reasoning. רב begins to show how a שרץ could be argued pure, and the argument itself comes on the next amud.

steps.title: The Rabbis count משה together with the seventy
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן finish their proof: the word 'with you' in the פסוק means משה is counted together with the seventy זקנים, which makes 71.
steps.simpleTranslation: '...with you.' 'With you' means: and you are counted with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing the proof of the רבנן that the סנהדרי גדולה has 71 judges. They read 'with you' as adding משה to the seventy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק tells משה to gather seventy זקנים who will stand 'with you'. The רבנן understand that משה is part of the group and not just standing next to it, so the total is 70 + 1 = 71.

keyTerms.meaning: And you are with them (counted among them)
The great סנהדרין, the highest court

phrases.english: "...with you" (במדבר 11:16).
"With you" means: and you are together with them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the source the רבנן brought on the previous page for 71 judges.
steps.raayaObject: The רבנן's view that the סנהדרי גדולה has 71 judges
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 11:16, 'and they shall stand there with you'

steps.title: רבי יהודה: 'with you' is about the שכינה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rejects the proof. 'With you' does not count משה as a judge. It tells משה to be present so that the שכינה would rest on the זקנים too.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה says: 'with you' is said because of the שכינה.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה, who holds there are only 70 judges, explains the same word a different way so that it does not add משה to the count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, משה stood with the זקנים so that the שכינה resting on him would also rest on them. Being present is not the same as being a member of the court, so the number stays at 70.

phrases.english: And רבי יהודה?
"With you" is said because of the Divine Presence.
phrases.notes: He means משה was there so the שכינה on him would rest on the זקנים too. It does not make him one of the judges.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reading in step 1 by explaining 'with you' differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from this word. It does not touch the רבנן's position itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'With you' can mean being present for the שכינה, not being counted as a judge.

steps.title: The Rabbis bring a second 'with you'
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן point to the next פסוק, 'and they shall bear the burden of the people with you'. Here 'with you' again means משה is counted together with them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? The פסוק says: 'And they shall bear the burden of the people with you.' 'With you' means: and you are with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The רבנן answer רבי יהודה with a different פסוק. This one is about judging together, not about the שכינה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carrying the burden of the people means judging them. If they carry it 'with you', משה is judging alongside them, so he is part of the court and the total is 71.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis? The verse says:
"And they shall bear the burden of the people with you" (במדבר 11:17).
"With you" means: and you are together with them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, אָמַר קְרָא: ״וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתְּךָ בְּמַשָּׂא הָעָם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After step 2 pushed aside the first 'with you', the רבנן bring a second one.
steps.raayaObject: That משה is counted with the seventy, making 71
steps.raayaSupportSource: במדבר 11:17, 'and they shall bear the burden of the people with you'

steps.title: רבי יהודה: 'with you' means 'like you'
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה reads this 'with you' as 'similar to you'. The judges must be like משה, so the word does not add משה to the count.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יהודה says: 'with you' means similar to you.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה again explains away the word 'with you' so that it does not count משה as a judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, the word teaches what kind of people the judges must be: like משה, of proper family and without blemish. It does not teach how many judges there are, so the number stays at 70.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to you, people like you

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבי יהודה made up a new law just to escape the proof. 'Similar to you' is a real requirement, and the רבנן agree with it. In the next step they only argue about which פסוק it comes from.

phrases.english: And רבי יהודה?
"With you" means: people similar to you.
phrases.notes: The judges must be like משה, from a proper family and without blemish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the second proof from step 3.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from the second 'with you'.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word teaches what the judges must be like, not how many there are.

steps.title: The Rabbis learn 'similar to you' from a different פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן learn 'similar to you' from the פסוק about the judges appointed on יתרו's advice. The סנהדרי גדולה learns from the smaller courts. That leaves 'with you' in במדבר free to teach that משה is counted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן? They learn it from 'and make it easier for you, and they shall bear it with you.' And the Great Sanhedrin learns from the lesser Sanhedrin.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the רבנן deal with רבי יהודה's point: they agree to the 'similar to you' law but get it from somewhere else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judges appointed in the time of יתרו also carried the burden 'with you' (שמות 18:22), and that is where the רבנן learn 'similar to you'. The rule then carries over from those smaller courts to the סנהדרי גדולה. So the 'with you' in במדבר is not needed for that law, and it can teach that משה joins the count, making 71.

keyTerms.meaning: A lesser court; here, the judges appointed in the time of יתרו

steps.whatToRemember: The whole מחלוקת turns on the word 'with you'. For the רבנן it adds משה, so there are 71 judges. For רבי יהודה it means 'for the שכינה' or 'like you', so there are 70. Both sides agree the judges must be 'similar to' משה. They only disagree about which פסוק teaches it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic way the גמרא defends a reading: once a law can be learned from another source, the word in question is free to teach something new.

phrases.english: And the Rabbis?
phrases.notes: He means: where do the רבנן get the law that judges must be 'similar to you'?

phrases.english: They derive it from "And they shall make it easier for you, and bear the burden with you" (שמות 18:22).
And the Great Sanhedrin learns from the lesser Sanhedrin.
phrases.notes: The 'lesser Sanhedrin' here means the judges appointed in the time of יתרו.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּנַן, מִ״וְהָקֵל מֵעָלֶיךָ וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתָּךְ״ נָפְקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי יהודה's reading in step 4 by moving the 'similar to you' law to another פסוק.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternate source: the law is learned from a different פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since 'with you' in במדבר teaches 'similar to you', it cannot also count משה.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Similar to you' comes from שמות 18:22 and carries over to the סנהדרי גדולה. The 'with you' in במדבר therefore counts משה, making 71.

steps.title: The two men who remained in the camp
steps.stepSummary: A new topic: a ברייתא about אלדד ומידד, who 'remained in the camp'. One opinion says they remained in the lottery box, meaning their names were not chosen.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: 'And two men remained in the camp.' Some say: they remained in the box.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new discussion about the appointment of the seventy זקנים. It quotes a ברייתא that explains what 'remained' means for אלדד ומידד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the 'יש אומרים', the זקנים were picked by lottery from a box. אלדד and מידד were the two whose names were not drawn. The next steps explain how the lottery worked, and step 11 brings רבי שמעון's different view.

keyTerms.meaning: A box or urn used for drawing lots

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
"And there remained two men in the camp" (במדבר 11:26).
Some say: they remained in the box.
phrases.notes: He means their names stayed in the box and were not picked for the seventy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic, connected only because it also deals with the appointment of the seventy זקנים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One opinion holds that אלדד ומידד 'remained' in the lottery box, meaning their names were not chosen.

steps.title: משה's problem: seventy does not divide evenly among twelve tribes
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא explains the background to the lottery. Any way משה divides seventy places among twelve tribes, something goes wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: When ה׳ told משה to gather seventy elders, משה asked how to do it. Six per tribe gives two too many. Five per tribe leaves ten missing. Six from some tribes and five from others will make the tribes jealous of each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא is explaining why אלדד ומידד 'remained in the box.' It lays out משה's problem, setting up the solution in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are twelve tribes and seventy places. Twelve times six is seventy-two, two too many. Twelve times five is sixty, ten too few. Giving some tribes more places than others is unfair and would cause jealousy, so משה needs a fair method.

keyTerms.meaning: Seventy men of the elders of Israel, the group ה׳ told משה to gather

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: For at the time that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:
"Gather for Me seventy men of the elders of Israel"
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:16

phrases.english: Moshe said: How shall I do this?
If I choose six from each and every tribe,
there will be two extra.

phrases.aramaic: אֶבְרוֹר חֲמִשָּׁה חֲמִשָּׁה מִכׇּל שֵׁבֶט וְשֵׁבֶט –
phrases.english: If I choose five each from each and every tribe,
there will be ten missing.

phrases.aramaic: אֶבְרוֹר שִׁשָּׁה מִשֵּׁבֶט זֶה וַחֲמִשָּׁה מִשֵּׁבֶט זֶה –
phrases.english: If I choose six from this tribe and five from that tribe,
I will be causing jealousy between the tribes.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁבְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the background of the opinion that אלדד ומידד 'remained in the box'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seventy places cannot be divided fairly among twelve tribes by simple numbers.

steps.title: The lottery with two blank slips
steps.stepSummary: משה picked six from each tribe and held a lottery for the seventy places. Two slips were left blank, so nobody could blame משה.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה chose six from every tribe, seventy-two in all. He made seventy-two slips, seventy marked 'elder' and two blank, mixed them in a box, and had each candidate draw one. To anyone who drew 'elder' he said that Heaven had made him holy. To anyone who drew a blank he said that ה׳ did not want him, so there was nothing משה could do.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives משה's solution: a lottery that lets Heaven decide who is left out. This is what 'they remained in the box' means for אלדד ומידד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every tribe gets the same chance, so no tribe can feel cheated. Since the slips decide, the two who lose cannot blame משה. It was ה׳'s choice, not his.

keyTerms.meaning: Blank (a slip with nothing written on it)

steps.whatToRemember: משה took six from each tribe and used a lottery with two blank slips. That way the tribes stayed equal and Heaven chose who was left out. אלדד ומידד were the two left 'in the box.'

phrases.english: What did he do?
He chose six from each tribe,
and he brought seventy-two slips.
On seventy of them he wrote "Elder,"
and two he left blank.
He mixed them and put them in a box.
He said to them: Come and take your slips!
Anyone whose hand came up with "Elder,"
he said: Heaven has already made you holy.
Whoever came up with a blank,
he said: ה׳ does not want you;
what can I do for you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers משה's question 'how shall I do this?' from step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to choose seventy elders from twelve tribes fairly
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Choose six per tribe and run a lottery with seventy 'elder' slips and two blank slips

steps.title: A similar problem: which firstborns must pay five shekels
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא compares a second case. There were 273 more בכורות than לויים, and the extra ones had to pay five שקלים. How could משה decide who pays?
steps.simpleTranslation: You can say something similar about the פסוק 'take five shekels per head.' משה asked how to handle it. If he told a בכור to pay and go, the בכור would answer that a לוי had already redeemed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second case with the same kind of problem. Again it sets up the problem first, and the solution comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each לוי redeemed one בכור, but there were 273 more בכורות than לויים. Those extra בכורות had to pay five שקלים. Any בכור משה picked could argue that he was one of the redeemed ones, so משה needed a method no one could argue with.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to this matter, introduces a parallel case

phrases.english: Similarly, you can say:
"And you shall take five shekels per head."
phrases.notes: במדבר 3:47. This is about the 273 בכורות who were more than the number of לויים.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מֹשֶׁה: כֵּיצַד אֶעֱשֶׂה לָהֶן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל?
phrases.english: Moshe said: How shall I do this for Israel?

phrases.aramaic: אִם אוֹמַר לוֹ: תֵּן לִי פִּדְיוֹנְךָ וָצֵא,
phrases.english: If I say to one: Give me your redemption money and go,

phrases.aramaic: יֹאמַר לִי: כְּבָר פְּדָאַנִי בֶּן לֵוִי.
phrases.english: he will say to me: A Levite already redeemed me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a parallel case where the same lottery idea applies
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With 273 extra בכורות, singling out any one בכור to pay would seem unfair to him.

steps.title: The lottery for the firstborns
steps.stepSummary: משה made 22,000 slips marked 'Levite' and 273 marked 'five shekels' and had the בכורות draw. The lottery decided who had to pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה made 22,000 slips saying 'Levite' and 273 saying 'five shekels,' mixed them in a box, and told the בכורות to draw. To anyone who drew 'Levite' he said a לוי had already redeemed him. To anyone who drew 'five shekels' he said to pay his redemption money and go.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives משה's solution: the same lottery method as with the elders. Heaven decides who pays, so no one can complain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 22,000 slips match the number of לויים, and the 273 slips match the extra בכורות. Since the slip decides, a בכור who must pay cannot claim a לוי redeemed him. This is the same idea as the blank slips for the elders.

keyTerms.meaning: Twenty-two thousand, the number of לויים
Two hundred seventy-three, the extra בכורות
Five shekels, the redemption price for a בכור

steps.whatToRemember: Both stories use the same idea. When there is no fair way to pick, משה used a lottery so that Heaven made the choice and no one could blame him.

phrases.english: What did he do?
He brought twenty-two thousand slips,
phrases.notes: This matches the number of לויים, one slip for each לוי.

phrases.english: and wrote on them "Levite,"
and on two hundred seventy-three more
he wrote "Five shekels."
He mixed them and put them in a box.
He said to them: Take your slips.
Whoever came up with "Levite,"

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ: כְּבָר פְּדָאֲךָ בֶּן לֵוִי.
phrases.english: he said to him: A Levite has already redeemed you.
Whoever came up with "Five shekels,"
he said to him: Pay your redemption money and go.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers משה's question from step 9 with the same lottery method used in step 8
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How to pick which 273 בכורות must pay without anyone claiming he was already redeemed
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A lottery of 22,000 'Levite' slips and 273 'five shekels' slips

steps.title: רבי שמעון: They stayed in the camp out of humility
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון explains that אלדד ומידד stayed in the camp because they felt unworthy of becoming זקנים, so הקב״ה promised to give them extra greatness.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: they stayed in the camp. When הקב״ה told משה to gather seventy men, אלדד ומידד said, 'We are not worthy of this greatness.' הקב״ה said, 'Since you made yourselves small, I will add greatness to your greatness.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives a second opinion on what 'they remained in the camp' means. רבי שמעון says they really stayed in the camp because they were humble.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion (Step 6) said they 'remained' in the lottery box, meaning they were not picked. רבי שמעון says they never entered the lottery at all; they held back out of humility. Because of that humility, הקב״ה promised them more.

keyTerms.meaning: You made yourselves small, you were humble

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
They remained in the camp.

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה
phrases.english: At the time that the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:
"Gather for Me seventy men,"
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:16

phrases.english: Eldad and Medad said:
We are not worthy of that greatness.
The Holy One, Blessed be He, said:
Since you made yourselves small,
I will add greatness onto your greatness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of Step 6 and gives רבי שמעון's alternative reading of 'remained in the camp'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אלדד ומידד stayed in the camp out of humility, and הקב״ה promised them added greatness.

steps.title: What extra greatness did they get?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks what the added greatness was.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what greatness did He add to them?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks a short question to set up its next line: what exactly was the extra reward?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 promised 'greatness on top of greatness' but did not say what it was. This question asks for that detail.

phrases.english: And what greatness did He add to them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the content of the promise made in Step 11.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the 'added greatness' given to אלדד ומידד was.

steps.title: Their prophecy never stopped
steps.stepSummary: All the other prophets (the זקנים) prophesied and then stopped, but אלדד ומידד kept prophesying.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the other prophets prophesied and then stopped, but they prophesied and did not stop.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers: the reward was that their prophecy kept going.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seventy זקנים got prophecy for a short time only. אלדד ומידד, who held back, got prophecy that lasted. Their humility brought a bigger gift than the position they turned down.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי שמעון, אלדד ומידד's humility was rewarded with prophecy that did not stop.
steps.confusionAlert: 'All the prophets' here does not mean every prophet in history. It means the other זקנים who got prophecy at that time.

phrases.english: That all the prophets prophesied and stopped,
phrases.notes: He means the other זקנים, who got prophecy at the same time.

phrases.english: but they prophesied and did not stop.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Their prophecy continued while the other זקנים' prophecy stopped.

steps.title: What did they prophesy?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the content of אלדד ומידד's prophecy was.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what prophecy did they prophesy?
steps.whatsHappening: Since we just heard that אלדד ומידד were prophets, the גמרא asks what they actually said. This sets up a list of opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says they prophesied in the camp but does not say what they said. The next steps give three different answers.

phrases.english: And what prophecy did they prophesy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the fact that they were prophets and asks what their prophecy contained.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The content of אלדד ומידד's prophecy.

steps.title: First view: משה will die and יהושע will lead
steps.stepSummary: They prophesied that משה would die and יהושע would bring ישראל into the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said: משה will die, and יהושע will bring ישראל into the land.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the first answer: their prophecy was about the change of leadership.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to this view, they foretold that משה would not enter ארץ ישראל and that יהושע would lead the people in.

phrases.english: They said: Moshe will die,
Yehoshua will bring Israel into the land.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They prophesied משה's death and יהושע's leadership.

steps.title: Second view: the quail
steps.stepSummary: אבא חנין in the name of רבי אליעזר says they prophesied about the quail.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבא חנין says in the name of רבי אליעזר: they prophesied about the quail, saying 'Rise up, quail! Rise up, quail!'
steps.whatsHappening: A second opinion: their prophecy was about the quail that came to feed the people right afterward.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This view connects their prophecy to the story right around it in the פסוקים, where ישראל asked for meat and the quail came. They called out for the quail to come up.

phrases.aramaic: אַבָּא חָנִין אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר:
phrases.english: Abba Chanin says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer:
They were prophesying about the matter of the quail:
Rise up, quail! Rise up, quail!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַבָּא חָנִין אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer to the question of Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They prophesied about the coming of the quail.

steps.title: Third view: גוג ומגוג, with a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says they prophesied about the war of גוג ומגוג, and brings a פסוק from יחזקאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן says: they prophesied about גוג ומגוג, as it says: 'So says ה׳: Are you the one I spoke about in early days, through My servants the prophets of ישראל, who prophesied in those days for years, that I would bring you upon them?'
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion: their prophecy was about the war of גוג ומגוג at the end of days. רב נחמן quotes a פסוק to support this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says that earlier prophets already spoke about גוג. On its own it does not name אלדד ומידד, so the next step shows how the פסוק points to them.

keyTerms.meaning: The nations of the great war at the end of days

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:

phrases.aramaic: עַל עִסְקֵי גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג הָיוּ מִתְנַבְּאִין,
phrases.english: They were prophesying about the matter of Gog and Magog,
as it says:
"So says ה׳, God:
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 38:17

phrases.aramaic: הַאַתָּה הוּא אֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתִּי בְּיָמִים קַדְמוֹנִים
phrases.english: Are you the one I spoke about in early days
through My servants, the prophets of Israel,
who prophesied in those days for years
that I would bring you upon them, etc."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר: עַל עִסְקֵי גּוֹג וּמָגוֹג הָיוּ מִתְנַבְּאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a third answer to Step 14 and brings a פסוק for it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They prophesied about the war of גוג ומגוג.

steps.title: Reading 'years' as 'two'
steps.stepSummary: The word שָׁנִים (years) is read as שְׁנַיִם (two). The two prophets who said the same prophecy at the same time are אלדד ומידד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Don't read it 'years', read it 'two'. Who are the two prophets who said one prophecy at one time? It must be אלדד ומידד.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן shows how the פסוק points to אלדד ומידד: by reading the word as 'two'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the reading 'two', the פסוק speaks of two prophets who prophesied about גוג together. The only known pair who prophesied the same thing at the same time is אלדד ומידד, so the prophecy about גוג was theirs.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read it as (a way of reading a word differently to learn something)
You must say, it must be

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common tool of the גמרא, אל תיקרי: reading a word with different vowels to uncover a hidden message in the פסוק.

phrases.english: Do not read "years" but "two."
phrases.notes: Same letters, different vowels: שָׁנִים means 'years' and שְׁנַיִם means 'two'.

phrases.english: Who are the two prophets
who prophesied one prophecy at one time?
You must say: Eldad and Medad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב נחמן's proof by rereading a word in the פסוק of Step 17.
steps.raayaObject: That אלדד ומידד prophesied about גוג ומגוג.

steps.title: How do we know the others stopped?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's line that the other prophets stopped and asks where that comes from.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: all the prophets prophesied and stopped, but they prophesied and did not stop. How do we know the others stopped?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line of the ברייתא (Step 13) and asks for its source: how do we know the other זקנים stopped prophesying?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא said this as a plain fact. The גמרא wants to know which פסוק teaches that the זקנים' prophecy ended.

phrases.english: The Master said:
All the prophets prophesied and stopped,
but they prophesied and did not stop.
From where do we know that they stopped?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: כׇּל הַנְּבִיאִים כּוּלָּן נִתְנַבְּאוּ וּפָסְקוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא's line in Step 13 and asks for its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source showing that the other זקנים stopped prophesying.

steps.title: Suggested source: 'ולא יספו'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the source is the פסוק 'they prophesied and did not continue'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say it is from the פסוק 'and they prophesied, ולא יספו (and did not continue)'...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a possible source, but it is only a suggestion. It sets up the next step, which will knock it down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain meaning of 'ולא יספו' seems to be 'they did not add more', meaning they stopped. The word אילימא tells us a challenge is coming.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (a suggestion that is about to be rejected)
And they did not continue (or: did not stop)

phrases.english: If you say it is from what is written:
"And they prophesied, and did not continue"?
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:25

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible answer to the question of Step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A suggestion that 'ולא יספו' (במדבר 11:25) shows they stopped.

steps.title: 'ולא יסף' at הר סיני means it did not stop
steps.stepSummary: The suggestion is rejected: by הר סיני the Torah says 'a great voice, ולא יסף', and there it must mean the voice did not stop.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, about 'a great voice, ולא יסף', would you also say the voice did not continue? No! It means it did not stop!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion. The same word appears at מתן תורה, and there it clearly means 'did not stop'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'ולא יסף' by הר סיני means the great voice never stopped, then 'ולא יספו' by the זקנים could also mean they never stopped. So this פסוק does not prove the זקנים stopped; it might even suggest the opposite.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (pointing out a strange result)
So too? Would you say the same?

steps.confusionAlert: The word יסף can come from 'add' (לא הוסיף, did not add) or from 'end' (סוף, did not end). These are opposite meanings, and that is the whole point of this step.

phrases.english: But if so:
"A great voice, and it did not continue" —
phrases.notes: דברים 5:19, about the voice at הר סיני.

phrases.english: would you also say it means the voice did not continue?
Rather, it means it did not stop!
phrases.notes: Here יָסָף is read like סוף, 'end': the voice had no end.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the source suggested in Step 20.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects 'ולא יספו' as proof that the זקנים stopped prophesying.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'ולא יסף' can mean 'did not stop', as it clearly does about the voice at הר סיני. So the פסוק does not prove the זקנים stopped.

steps.title: A new source: the seventy stopped, but אלדד ומידד kept going
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proves from the difference between 'ויתנבאו' (past tense) and 'מתנבאים' (present tense) that the seventy זקנים stopped prophesying while אלדד ומידד kept on.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, about the seventy זקנים the פסוק says 'they prophesied', and about אלדד ומידד it says 'they are prophesying'. So אלדד ומידד were still prophesying on and on.
steps.whatsHappening: Step 21 rejected the first source, so the גמרא now gives a new one. It compares the verb used for the seventy זקנים with the verb used for אלדד ומידד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'ויתנבאו' is past tense: it happened and was over. 'מתנבאים' is present tense: still going on. That contrast shows the seventy stopped and אלדד ומידד did not, which answers the question from step 19.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof is from grammar: past tense for the seventy (they stopped), present tense for אלדד ומידד (they kept going).

phrases.english: Rather, here it is written: "They prophesied,"
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:25, about the seventy זקנים.

phrases.english: there it is written: "are prophesying."
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:27, about אלדד ומידד in the camp.

phrases.english: They were still prophesying, on and on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the source that was rejected in step 21.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The difference between past tense 'ויתנבאו' and present tense 'מתנבאים' shows the seventy stopped and אלדד ומידד continued.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where do we learn that the other prophets stopped (step 19)?

steps.title: Why did יהושע want them imprisoned, if they didn't say משה would die?
steps.stepSummary: The 'משה will die' opinion explains יהושע's alarm. The other two opinions seem to leave it unexplained.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense if they prophesied 'משה will die'; that is why יהושע said 'My master משה, imprison them.' But according to the other two opinions, why would יהושע say that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests the opinions about what אלדד ומידד prophesied against יהושע's reaction in the פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A prophecy that משה will die and יהושע will lead sounds like a threat to משה, so יהושע's anger fits. If they only prophesied about the quail or about גוג ומגוג, nothing in it touches משה. So why would יהושע want them stopped?

keyTerms.meaning: according to the one who says

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says they prophesied "משה will die,"
that is why it is written: "My master משה, imprison them."
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:28. יהושע is the one saying this.

phrases.english: But according to the one who says those other two,
phrases.notes: The other two opinions: they prophesied about the quail, or about גוג ומגוג.

phrases.english: what is "My master משה, imprison them"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the question of whether they kept prophesying to testing the opinions about what they prophesied.
steps.kashyaTarget: The two opinions that their prophecy was about the quail or about גוג ומגוג.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the prophecy had nothing to do with משה, יהושע had no reason to ask that they be stopped.

steps.title: Prophesying near משה was disrespectful
steps.stepSummary: Even if the prophecy wasn't about משה, giving it publicly near him was like a student ruling on הלכה in front of his teacher.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is not proper behavior. It is like a student who rules on הלכה in front of his teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 23: יהושע objected to the way they prophesied, not to what they said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was respect, not content. Prophesying in public right near משה, the leader of the generation, is like a student giving rulings in front of his רבי. That is why יהושע wanted them held back.

keyTerms.meaning: a student who rules on הלכה in front of his teacher

phrases.english: Because it is not proper conduct,
for it is like a student
who rules on halacha in front of his teacher.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shifts the objection from the content of the prophecy to the manner of giving it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יהושע's objection must have been about what they said, which only fits 'משה will die'.
steps.terutzMaskana: יהושע objected because prophesying near משה was disrespectful, so the other two opinions also work.

steps.title: Would משה wish everyone prophesied his death?
steps.stepSummary: משה's reply 'would that all the people were prophets' fits the other two opinions. But how could משה welcome a prophecy of his own death?
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense according to the other two opinions; that is why משה said 'Would that all the people were prophets.' But if they prophesied that משה will die, would he have been happy with that?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the challenge flips: משה's warm answer fits the other two opinions, but seems to clash with the 'משה will die' opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the prophecy was about the quail or about גוג ומגוג, משה wishing everyone could prophesy makes sense. If the prophecy was that he would die and יהושע would take over, it seems strange for משה to wish everyone would say such things.

keyTerms.meaning: it would please him / be fine with him

phrases.english: Granted, according to the one who says those other two,
that is why it is written: "Would that..."
phrases.notes: במדבר 11:29: משה wishes that all of ה׳'s people were prophets.

phrases.english: But according to the one who says "משה will die,"
would that have been pleasing to him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirror image of step 23: now the 'משה will die' opinion is the one being challenged.
steps.kashyaTarget: The opinion that אלדד ומידד prophesied 'משה will die'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: משה would not wish for everyone to prophesy his own death, yet he said 'מי יתן'.

steps.title: משה didn't hear what they said
steps.stepSummary: The prophecy was not finished in front of משה, so he did not know its content.
steps.simpleTranslation: They did not finish telling it in front of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 25: משה only knew that they were prophesying, not what they were saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's reply was about the fact that they were prophesying, not about the message itself. Since he never heard the part about his death, 'מי יתן' does not contradict the 'משה will die' opinion.

keyTerms.meaning: they did not finish it in front of him

phrases.english: They did not finish it in front of him.
phrases.notes: משה only heard that they were prophesying, not the full message.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits what משה knew at the time.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משה knew the prophecy was about his death and still said 'מי יתן'.
steps.terutzMaskana: משה did not hear the content, so all three opinions fit the פסוקים.
steps.whatToRemember: Each side gets one challenge and one answer: the 'משה will die' view on its own, and the other two views together. יהושע objected out of respect for משה (step 24), and משה didn't know the content (step 26).

steps.title: What does 'כלאם' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what יהושע actually meant by 'כלאם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'imprison them' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the word 'כלאם' means, setting up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Taken literally, 'כלאם' sounds like a harsh request to lock them up. The גמרא wants to know what יהושע really meant.

phrases.english: What is "imprison them"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the word 'כלאם' quoted in step 23 and asks for its meaning.

steps.title: Keep them busy with community needs
steps.stepSummary: יהושע told משה to give them public responsibilities, and their prophesying would stop on its own.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Put the needs of the community on them, and they will stop on their own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that 'כלאם' was not a call to jail them. It meant to load them with communal work so their prophecy would fade away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'כלאם' is read as connected to 'כָּלִין', ending. Communal burdens would keep them so busy that they would stop prophesying naturally, without anyone forcing them.

keyTerms.meaning: they come to an end on their own

steps.whyThisMatters: It turns a harsh-sounding word into a gentle plan, and it teaches that heavy public responsibility can push aside even a gift like prophecy.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַטֵּל עֲלֵיהֶן צׇרְכֵי צִיבּוּר,
phrases.english: He said to him: Place the needs of the community upon them,
phrases.notes: יהושע is the one speaking to משה.

phrases.english: and they will come to an end on their own.
phrases.notes: Wordplay: 'כלאם' is read like 'כָּלִין', ending.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הַטֵּל עֲלֵיהֶן צׇרְכֵי צִיבּוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'כלאם' means: burden them with community needs and they will stop prophesying on their own.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: יהושע did not want them jailed. He wanted their prophecy to end naturally through public responsibility.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה: Where do the three extra judges come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's question about the source for adding three judges beyond twenty, to begin a new discussion.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn to bring three more judges?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה as a heading. This sets up the next move, which will challenge the משנה's answer to this question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה learned twenty judges from two verses that each say עדה (a group of ten). It then asked where the extra three come from. Its answer was that convicting needs a majority of two. Now the גמרא is about to test that answer.

phrases.english: From where [do we learn] to bring three more?
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה. Twenty judges were already learned from two verses, so we need a source for the last three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of אלדד and מידד and returns to the משנה's count of judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה asks for the source of the three extra judges in a court of twenty-three.

steps.title: A majority of exactly two is impossible with twenty-three judges
steps.stepSummary: With twenty-three judges, a guilty majority is either one or three, never exactly two.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, you can never find a majority of two for conviction. If eleven acquit and twelve convict, the majority is still only one. If ten acquit and thirteen convict, the majority is three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's answer. With twenty-three judges, the numbers never produce a majority of exactly two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Twenty-three is an odd number, so the gap between the two sides is always odd: one, three, and so on. The משנה said we need twenty-three judges to make a majority of two possible. But with twenty-three, that exact majority can never happen.

phrases.aramaic: סוֹף סוֹף, לְרָעָה עַל פִּי שְׁנַיִם
phrases.english: Ultimately, [a majority] for conviction by two
you cannot find it.
If eleven acquit
and twelve convict,
it is still [a majority of] one.
If ten acquit
and thirteen convict,
they are [a majority of] three.

steps.triggerLanguage: סוֹף סוֹף, לְרָעָה עַל פִּי שְׁנַיִם לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the משנה's answer to the question quoted in Step 29.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's claim that twenty-three judges are needed for a majority of two to convict.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Arithmetic: an odd number of judges can never produce a gap of exactly two.

steps.title: רבי אבהו: It happens when judges are added, or in a court of seventy
steps.stepSummary: A majority of two is possible after judges are added, and also in the סנהדרי גדולה according to רבי יהודה, who counts seventy judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said: You only find it when judges are added, and that works according to everyone. You also find it in the סנהדרי גדולה, according to רבי יהודה, who says it has seventy judges.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו shows real cases where a majority of exactly two can happen. In each case the number of voting judges is even.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a judge says 'I don't know,' two judges are added, which leaves an even number of judges actually voting. That makes a gap of two possible, and every opinion agrees it works. It is also possible in the סנהדרי גדולה if, like רבי יהודה, you count seventy judges, which is an even number.
steps.whatToRemember: A majority of exactly two needs an even number of voting judges. That happens once judges are added, or in a court of seventy according to רבי יהודה.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said: You do not find [it]
except when they add [judges], and this is according to everyone,
phrases.notes: Judges are added when one judge says 'I don't know.' That leaves an even number of judges actually voting.

phrases.english: and in the Great Sanhedrin,
according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says [it has] seventy.
phrases.notes: The other view counts seventy-one. Seventy is even, so a majority of two can happen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: אִי אַתָּה מוֹצֵא אֶלָּא בְּמוֹסִיפִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the arithmetic challenge in Step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the scenario to specific cases with an even number of voting judges.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A majority of two can never happen, so the משנה's reasoning seems empty.
steps.terutzMaskana: It does happen when judges are added, and in a seventy-member סנהדרין according to רבי יהודה.

steps.title: רבי אבהו: After adding judges, the court is even-numbered from the start
steps.stepSummary: When judges are added, an even-numbered court is formed from the outset.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו also said: When judges are added, they make an even-numbered court from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבהו gives a second rule. Adding judges creates an even-numbered court, and this is allowed from the start.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a court should have an odd number of judges so it cannot split evenly. רבי אבהו says that after judges are added, we knowingly allow an even-numbered court.

keyTerms.meaning: An even-numbered court, one that can split evenly

phrases.english: And Rabbi Abbahu said:
When they add [judges], they make
an even-numbered court from the start.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ: בְּמוֹסִיפִין עוֹשִׂין בֵּית דִּין שָׁקוּל לְכַתְּחִילָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A related rule from the same אמורא about adding judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: After adding judges, the court may be even-numbered from the outset.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי אבהו needed to say this at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי אבהו's rule as something too obvious to need saying. This sets up the next step, which shows what it teaches.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once one judge has said 'I don't know' and two judges are added, the court that is actually voting is plainly even: 22 plus 2 makes 24. So what new point is רבי אבהו making? The next step explains it.

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why the rule in Step 32 was needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's statement that an even court is formed after adding judges.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With the 'I don't know' judge out and two judges added, the voting court is obviously even, so the statement seems to teach nothing.

steps.title: A judge who said 'I don't know' counts as gone
steps.stepSummary: The new point is that the judge who said 'I don't know' is treated as absent. Even if he later gives a reason, he is not counted.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought that the judge who said 'I don't know' is still treated as present, so if he says something later we listen to him. רבי אבהו teaches that he is treated as absent, so if he later gives a reason we do not listen to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the hidden point in רבי אבהו's rule. The judge who said 'I don't know' is out completely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If that judge could return to the vote, the court would really be odd-numbered again. By saying the court is even, רבי אבהו shows the judge has no vote anymore, even if he later comes up with a reason.

keyTerms.meaning: He is like someone who is not there

steps.whatToRemember: A judge who says 'I don't know' leaves the vote for good. That is why the court becomes truly even-numbered.

phrases.english: You might have said: this one who says 'I do not know'
is like one who is [still] there,
and if he says something, we listen to him;
so he teaches us
that this one who says 'I do not know'
is like one who is not there,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמַר טַעְמָא – לָא שָׁמְעִינַן לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: and if he says a reason, we do not listen to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge in Step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: מהו דתימא: shows a reasonable mistake the rule prevents.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The judge who said 'I don't know' still counts and can rejoin the vote, so the court is really odd-numbered.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is treated as absent, and his later reasons are ignored, so the court is truly even-numbered.

steps.title: רב כהנא: If every judge convicts, the defendant goes free
steps.stepSummary: If the entire סנהדרין votes to convict in a capital case, the defendant is acquitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: If a סנהדרין all saw him as guilty, they let him go free.
steps.whatsHappening: A new rule begins. רב כהנא says a unanimous guilty vote leads to acquittal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This sounds backwards, since everyone agrees he is guilty. The reason comes in the next steps.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean a unanimous court is mistaken about the facts. The issue is that the trial process requires the possibility of someone arguing for acquittal.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said:
A Sanhedrin where all of them saw [him] as guilty,
they acquit him.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב כָּהֲנָא: סַנְהֶדְרִי שֶׁרָאוּ כּוּלָּן לְחוֹבָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic about voting in capital cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A unanimous guilty vote in a capital case results in acquittal.

steps.title: What is the reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב כהנא's surprising rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a unanimous guilty vote should free the defendant. This sets up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule seems to go against common sense, so the גמרא wants its logic spelled out.

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the logic behind Step 35.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reasoning behind acquitting when all the judges convict.

steps.title: The overnight delay exists to find merit, and these judges will find none
steps.stepSummary: We have a tradition that a verdict is delayed overnight to search for merit. A court that is completely set on guilt will never find any.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have a tradition that the verdict is held overnight to give a chance to find merit for him. These judges will no longer see any merit for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רב כהנא's rule using the required overnight delay before a guilty verdict.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A conviction cannot be given on the same day, so that someone might think of a reason to acquit overnight. When every judge is already fixed on guilt, that purpose can never be met. So the conviction cannot go through.

keyTerms.meaning: We have a tradition, we learned

steps.whatToRemember: In capital cases, the system needs a real chance for someone to argue for acquittal. Without that chance, there is no conviction.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that in capital cases the process itself protects the defendant, not just the vote count.

phrases.english: Since we have a tradition [that] holding the verdict overnight
phrases.notes: A guilty verdict in a capital case has to wait until the next day.

phrases.english: is to create merit for him,
and these [judges] will no longer see [any merit] for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דִּגְמִירִי הֲלָנַת דִּין לְמֶעְבַּד לֵיהּ זְכוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in Step 36.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The overnight delay exists to find merit. A unanimous guilty court will never find any, so the defendant goes free.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's list of qualities for a סנהדרין judge
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that only people of stature, wisdom, good appearance and suitable age, who understand כישוף and know seventy languages, may sit on the סנהדרין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: Only men who are tall, wise, good-looking and of the right age are placed on the סנהדרין. They must also understand כישוף and know seventy languages, so the סנהדרין never has to hear testimony through a translator.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement from רבי יוחנן listing the qualities a person needs to be seated on the סנהדרין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first four traits (stature, wisdom, appearance, age) make the court respected. The last two are practical skills. Understanding כישוף lets the judges rule on sorcerers, and knowing many languages means they hear witnesses directly instead of through a translator.

keyTerms.meaning: They seat (appoint) someone as a judge
The great court of seventy-one judges
People who understand how sorcery works
Seventy languages, meaning all the world's languages

steps.confusionAlert: בעלי כשפים does not mean the judges practice sorcery. It means they understand it well enough to judge people accused of it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says:
They do not seat on the Sanhedrin
anyone except men of tall stature,
and men of wisdom, and men of good appearance,
and men of suitable age,
and masters of sorcery,
phrases.notes: He means they understand how sorcery works, so they can judge sorcerers.

phrases.english: and men who know seventy languages,
so that the Sanhedrin will not be
hearing testimony from the mouth of a translator.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אֵין מוֹשִׁיבִין בְּסַנְהֶדְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from how the סנהדרין votes to who is qualified to sit on it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סנהדרין judge must have stature, wisdom, good appearance and suitable age, must understand כישוף, and must know seventy languages so the court never relies on a translator.

steps.title: A judge must be able to argue that a שרץ is pure
steps.stepSummary: רב, quoted by רב יהודה, rules that only someone who can build a Torah-based argument that a שרץ is pure may sit on the סנהדרין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה says in the name of רב: Only someone who knows how to prove from the Torah that a שרץ is pure may be placed on the סנהדרין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second qualification. The judge must have extremely sharp reasoning skills.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah clearly says a שרץ is impure, so the point is not to change the law. A judge must be skilled enough in logical argument to build a convincing case even for something false. Then he can recognize and take apart clever but wrong arguments in court.

keyTerms.meaning: To declare or prove something pure
A creeping creature whose carcass the Torah calls impure
From the Torah itself, using its own sources and logic

steps.confusionAlert: רב is not saying a שרץ is actually pure. It is a test of sharp reasoning, not a ruling.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda says that Rav says:
They do not seat on the Sanhedrin
anyone except one who knows how
to make a creeping animal pure from the Torah.
phrases.notes: The Torah plainly calls a שרץ impure. He means building a clever Torah-based argument that it's pure.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: אֵין מוֹשִׁיבִין בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another qualification for סנהדרין judges, this one about sharp reasoning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A סנהדרין judge must be skilled enough to build a Torah-based argument that a שרץ is pure.

steps.title: רב says he can make the argument himself
steps.stepSummary: רב declares that he will reason through the law of שרץ and show how it could be made pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: I will reason it out and show that it is pure.
steps.whatsHappening: רב announces that he can do this kind of reasoning himself. The גמרא is setting up the actual argument, which comes right after this line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line adds no new rule. It shows that the skill רב just described is something a real scholar can actually do. It opens the way for the proof that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: I will reason it out, I will argue the case
And I will make it pure

phrases.english: Rav said:
I will reason it out and make it pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רב shows that his own rule can be carried out by offering to do it himself. This sets up the proof that follows.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב claims he can build the argument that a שרץ is pure, introducing the demonstration that follows.
